utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Shin, we had reached a stage where I think you were going to deal with a point in private session. Do you want to go on from there, or do you want to go somewhere else to start with?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I thank Your Honours. I would prefer to begin in private session on that same point.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: The Prosecution will now turn to its third point regarding the guarantees offered by the Republic of Serbia and the state Serbia and Montenegro. I would begin here with the jurisprudence, because much was said here yesterday which was distorting of the law of jurisprudence of the Tribunal on this point and perhaps resulting from a misunderstanding of that jurisprudence. There is simply no question here of a blanket rejection of a guarantee of any particular state. The jurisprudence of this Tribunal states that guarantees - even strong, dependable ones - might be relied upon in some cases and not in others. Even guarantees from the same state. I would refer in particular to the Appeals Chamber's decision in the Mrksic provisional release application. In paragraph 9 of that decision, the Appeals Chamber stated quite clearly that "the reliability of a guarantee must be determined in relation to the circumstances of the individual case." To illustrate that principle, the Appeals Chamber went on to provide two examples. The first example was a hypothetical Accused A, who would have voluntarily surrendered upon learning of his indictment by this Tribunal and who may have cooperated with the Prosecution in a way which demonstrated genuine intention to return for trial. In contrast to this example, the Appeals Chamber offered hypothetical Accused B, a high-level government official at the time alleged to have committed the crimes charged, and secondly, in possession of valuable information which he could disclose to the Tribunal if minded to cooperate. The Appeals Chamber stated that it was reasonable for Trial Chambers to rely on the guarantee in the case of Accused A and not in the case of Accused B, even if that guarantee or those guarantees were to come from the same authorities. The principle to be distilled from that decision, we would submit, is that it is the personal attitude of the accused which of foremost importance, and to be the first matter considered in evaluating provisional release generally, and also in evaluating the weight to be given a state guarantee. I refer briefly to Trial Chamber I's hearing on Mr. Martic's provisional release application from September of last year in which Judge Orie indicated that the attitude of the accused is the main issue, suggesting that, if positive, the support of the government would certainly assist to convince the Court of provisional release, but in any case, His Honour Judge Orie emphasised that this attitude of the accused is the first step to be considered. In relation to points raised yesterday by the distinguished Mr. Caric representing Serbia and Montenegro, we would submit that Mr. Caric himself in his submissions bears out the approach of the Tribunal on this matter. He cited several cases of people who had sought provisional release here and had been granted provisional release by the various Trial Chambers of the Tribunal in which the state guarantees were in fact relied upon. He mentioned Ms. Plavsic, Mr. Miodrag Jokic, Mr. Talic, Mr. Pavle Strugar, and Mr. Gruban. So clearly there's no question here of dismissing wholesale any particular state's guarantee. We would submit that the distinction between those cases where the state guarantee was relied upon and those in which it was not is clearly discernible. In the cases cited, surrender occurred in a matter of days to months after the accused learned of the indictment against him or her, not, certainly, a matter of years. Further on Mr. Caric's representations yesterday, in response to his representations regarding the Rule 54 bis proceedings in another case, we would argue that that proceeding is in fact relevant to this provisional release hearing as that proceeding arises from a failure of cooperation or difficulties in cooperation from the authorities in Serbia and Serbia and Montenegro. The Appeals Chamber decision in Sainovic and Ojdanic from last year instructs that the degree of cooperation by state authorities is a relevant consideration for provisional release. Finally on Mr. Caric's representations, we note that he made a reference to six persons having been surrendered by Serbia or Serbia and Montenegro. And we would just seek some clarification on that, whether that is a matter distinct from the, as he calls them, voluntary surrenders which he mentioned elsewhere in his submissions. On the matter of the state guarantees, the Prosecution would otherwise rely on the submissions it has made in its response brief and refer briefly to one point in the jurisprudence of the Tribunal. Both the Sainovic/Ojdanic Appeals Chamber decision and also the Appeals Chamber in Mrksic point out -- in the Mrksic decision point to the relevance of circumstances at the time the accused would be expected to return for trial. The Appeals Chamber, of course, does not indicate that any speculation should occur, but rather that, to the extent possible, the context of the future was a relevant consideration, the Appeals Chamber in Mrksic specifically relating to the likelihood of future change in government as a factor to take into account. We would simply point out that, in light of recent developments, including the tragic assassination of Prime Minister Djindjic, and the transition of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia to its newly-constituted state, Serbia and Montenegro, and the current status of the president of Serbia as a caretaker president, among other matters, points or reflects these political uncertainties and, under the jurisprudence, further militates against the reliance on the state guarantees in this particular case, and we emphasise again "in this particular case with this particular accused." We would also point out that there are, as the assassination of Mr. Djindjic demonstrates, the real risks from anti-Tribunal forces in Serbia and Serbia Montenegro, as my learned colleague himself yesterday pointed out in relation to various media articles as well. I would just add one more to that. Mr. Mihajlovic, Dusan Mihajlovic, the Minister of the Interior of Serbia, himself was cited two days ago in the Belgrade VIP daily news service as indicating that the assassination was -- the criminal group that committed that assassination was connected to what is referred to as quasi-patriotic or anti-Hague elements in Serbia. And he is further cited for the point that the actual decision to carry out the assassination was made by a Mr. Spasojevic and a Legija, of whom mention was made yesterday, who called the terrorist plan "Stop The Hague." The fourth point the Prosecution would make relates to the senior position of the accused. The accused, obviously, was the former president of Serbia. He benefited from that position. And certainly in terms of protection from authorities from having to surrender or being transferred to this Tribunal, he seeks now to benefit further from that position through the various arguments made yesterday in relation to political stability and democratic transition and the alleged important role he played in that regard. However, the jurisprudence is to the contrary effect. A senior position of the accused militates against provisional release. As the Appeals Chamber in the Sainovic/Ojdanic decision noted, the position of an accused in the hierarchy and the consequence of that position upon the weight of government guarantees are significant factors, factors weighing against the granting of provisional release. My learned colleague suggested yesterday, listing several persons who had been granted provisional release, that high status in fact might not count as a factor against -- I'm sorry, a high factor would not be a factor that would militate against provisional release. I would simply reiterate that a review of those who have been granted provisional release and those who have not would indicate that it was not the high status of the accused that was so much a matter but, rather, the time between the recognition or knowledge of the indictment and the time of the surrender. I would turn now to the discretionary matter sought by the medical condition, and perhaps Your Honours would seek to go into private session on this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I would now just address quickly some further matters raised in the course of the hearing yesterday. With regards to the matter of public perception, I would submit that the documents set out in Annex 1 of the accused's application for provisional release are not relevant. Those and other documents may welcome the surrender of Mr. Milutinovic. We would submit that the surrender of Mr. Milutinovic is quite a different point from the provisional release of the accused and that the fact that there are persons who may welcome his surrender hardly indicates that they would actually call for his provisional release as well. Otherwise, we would merely point out that an important element of the public in this area of public perception of the Tribunal is, of course, first and foremost the victim groups. Otherwise, we would rely upon submissions we made in our response brief. Secondly, there was also a point raised with regards to the threat to victims, witnesses, and others. We would rely on our submissions in the response brief and simply point out a couple factors. First, that we would submit that the Prosecution need not on this point prove that such threats or other forms of danger to these persons has actually happened. We would rely on, among other points in the jurisprudence, on Blaskic in which the possession of disclosure materials was indicated as a factor increasing that risk, and also the decision of this Trial Chamber in Krajisnik, this Trial Chamber differently constituted, and noting, of course, the dissenting opinion of Your Honour Judge Robinson, including a dissent on that particular point. We would submit here again that what is principally important is the personal attitude of the accused, and that is that he has no respect for this institution, as he has demonstrated by his conduct and, we would submit, by his words. My learned colleague set out yesterday as an argument on this point "the reputation for integrity and public service." And I'm not sure if you'd want to go to closed session just for a very few points on this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And finally -- thank you. Finally, some brief comments on the matter of personal cooperation which is not controversial, we would submit. The Prosecution completely rejects the characterisation by my learned colleague that the policy of the Prosecution in any way represents an inducement to accused. The jurisprudence is very clear on this point. The Appeals Chamber in Sainovic and Ojdanic was absolutely clear, both in the majority and in the dissent. The Prosecution has also been very clear in its position in submissions both written and oral before this Trial Chamber. So just to make it plain, we would state again that the law in this area is settled, and the Prosecution follows, of course, that law. If I might just add one point before I move to my conclusion. I had cited yesterday a representation made in the provisional release hearing last year for Mr. Sainovic and Mr. Ojdanic regarding the arrest -- or rather, regarding the policy of Serbia not to transfer Mr. Milutinovic until the end of his term of president. That representation was made by Mr. Nebojsa Sarkic who was the assistant to the Federal Ministry of Justice at that time. And I believe that may be on page 46 of the transcript, although I'm not entirely sure. And we would just point out again that Mr. Sarkic on that occasion did state that the accused -- this accused would either voluntarily surrender after his term as president had terminated, or he would be transferred by coercion if necessary. And that, of course, touches also upon the nature of this accused's surrender. And we would submit that further reflects the fact that his surrender is not really voluntary as in the context of Rule 65(B) as he surrendered knowing that he may -- or believing full well he may otherwise be arrested. In conclusion, the Prosecution would simply state that the accused's surrender first of all was not voluntary within the meaning or the context of Rule 65(B). He was a fugitive refusing to surrender to this Tribunal for nearly four years. He acknowledged this Tribunal only when he had to; prior to that, expressing his disdain for this Tribunal both in his conduct and his words. He surrendered only when the protection he was enjoying from state authorities appeared to be coming to an end and when he believed that he would have no other choice and that it would be in his best self-interest to try to seek to gain some advantages from his voluntary surrender, including the provision of guarantees by his state. Therefore, the Prosecution would submit the personal guarantees of this accused can be given no weight. Under these circumstances, the Prosecution submits that the jurisprudence teaches that a state guarantee cannot cure his failure to persuade that he would return for trial, nor would conditions upon his release cure this failure. The medical condition of the accused, the arguments have been set out fully previously in this hearing. And finally, during the four-year period, the accused, we would submit, had no excuse in law, whether before October 2000 or after October 2000, and this point has essentially been conceded by my learned colleague. Under these circumstances, we would submit that the accused will always have a response -- always have a response and a reason why he should not attend at this Tribunal if given the choice, and that he would continue to seek such reasons and the circumstances in which he would be able to use those reasons not to attend at this Tribunal. Thank you, Your Honours. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Shin. Mr. Livingston, fairly briefly, if you would, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I just start by dealing with what I think has emerged as the key point in this motion. That is the -- in relation to the period after October 2000, as Mr. Shin put it yesterday. He says: "There is no authority that political considerations can justify defiance of Tribunal authority." He says: "Contribution to political stability should be given no weight." In my submission, those formulations put the emphasis in the wrong place. The issue, in my submission, is fundamental, and I think this is something that Judge Hunt emphasised in his, albeit dissenting judgement in the Ojdanic and Sainovic appeal motion. The question is: Does his behaviour demonstrate that he didn't intend to surrender? And in my submission, the evidence overwhelmingly which you have in this motion indicates that he did. Can I also say this: That I accept the point that the Appeals Chamber has made both in the Mrksic case and in the Ojdanic and Sainovic one, that one must look at each case, at each defendant on his own merits and in his own particular context. The passage of time perhaps sometimes dulls the memory, but I hope all of us in this courtroom can remember the dramatic pictures which crossed our television screens in October 2000, the storming of the parliament building, setting fire to the television station, looting, pictures of general disorder. It was a situation which could have descended rapidly into chaos had the authorities not got a grip on the situation very quickly. It was an exceptional situation which resulted from the fall of the previous regime. In a sense, one is seeing it again in Iraq on our television screens just recently. It's not a commonal garden political situation that's being put forward here. This was an emergency which Serbia faced at that time. And it's reflected -- it's not likely, in my submissions, that politicians of the standing of the late Dr. Djindjic, Mr. Milasinovic, Mr. Zivkovic, make the points that they do, that it was important for the stability of the country. It doesn't just -- the problem just doesn't go away in one day or one week or one month. It's important for the political stability of the country that this defendant served out his mandate. It's not meant to be an indication of showing disdain, as it's put, for this Tribunal. In that context, it shouldn't be forgotten --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Livingston, important for the stability, would you put it higher than that, it was indispensable?

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: Yes, I would put it higher than that. Yes, I would put it that high; yes, I would accept that phrase. I am reminded by Mr. Milutinovic, I think it's an important point, that when he was Foreign Minister, of course as he was before 1997, he was the person who established the first liaison office with the Tribunal in Belgrade. And that, in my submission, is not the mark of a man who was showing disdain for the jurisdiction of the Tribunal. He was a party to the start of cooperation with this Tribunal. And in my submission, it's an important point. A further important point which again Mr. Milutinovic reminds me of which I think it is important to make is this: Because he's a former president of Serbia, he will be under guard, and that is by bodyguards, protection, day and night, 24 hours a day, if he returns. He's entitled to that, and that is the position that he will have. I'm sure Mr. Caric, if asked, would confirm that. The possibility of him, therefore, disappearing into the woodwork where he can't be found is frankly nonexistent in his particular circumstances. And Mr. Caric made the point yesterday that the authorities have had no problems in enforcing any other guarantees that they have given for other defendants granted provisional release. The fact that this defendant will be under close guard and supervision all the time makes that -- makes it even less likely that there will be any problems about this defendant not surrendering in due course. It's an importance difference which he has from all, if not certainly virtually all, other defendants at this Tribunal. A point is made about the senior position of the accused. In my submission, what Mr. Shin says has come very close to accepting my point. He refers to various other accused of high rank who have been granted provisional release, and he says, well, in those particular cases, the high position was not such an important factor in the decision to grant provisional release, it's more a matter of the shortness of the period of time between knowledge of the indictment and surrender. I agree with the point, and in a sense, it's my point that the fact that there is a perceived high authority - and I stress the word "perceived," and you have my submissions on that from yesterday - is not a bar. I think Mr. Shin misrepresented my point. When I say it's not a bar to provisional release, the issue in the end, though, in my submission, is not simply a matter of the distance in time between knowledge of the indictment and surrender, it's a question of is the surrender voluntary? And if you are satisfied, as you have to be, that the surrender was voluntary in this particular case, then in my submission, the fact that that defendant is prima facie - and I stress the words prima facie - in a high position should not be a bar to his being granted provisional release. At the end of the day, the question is: Will he appear at court? Will he abide by any conditions which this Court imposes? Will he interfere with witnesses? In my submission, whether a defendant who is going to be guarded day and night, with a defendant who, frankly, has a record which I stand by on my submissions, in my submission, it's also inconceivable that he would, having surrendered once, not surrender and abide by conditions in the future. And I would invite you very strongly to that conclusion. I think I'm virtually at the end of my ten minutes. Can I just make one other point, very briefly, which is of concern to my client. He frankly denies having made the statement as it's attributed by the Prosecution in the Reuters report in January 2001. He also wishes me to make the point that Nacional as a paper has actually been closed down earlier this year by the new High Representative in Bosnia, Paddy Ashdown, one of the reasons being because of the unreliable nature of its reporting. So it no longer functions, that newspaper. But in my submission, the important point about that is that the Prosecution's acceptance that in recent times, and 2001 is a long time ago, the beginning of 2001, this defendant unequivocally, without going into the argument about what was said and what was meant by certain statements, unequivocally he's never shown the disdain which the Prosecution indicate. He has never indicated he wouldn't surrender. And in my submission, if you're able to conclude, as I submit, that what these very senior, honourable politicians in Serbia -- and we shouldn't forget they have been admitted to the Council of Europe recently -- the clear intention is to show praise for the behaviour of the current regime in Serbia in recent times. If you accept what they say, they're adamant this was a voluntary surrender, they're adamant that this defendant's serving out his mandate was indispensable, to use Judge Robinson's word, to the future of the country as from October 2000 onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: No, no, I understand that. I do understand that. I'm sorry if you thought I was imputing that to you. It was simply the word which I was adopting which was put to me, and I would respectfully suggest that is the picture which those politicians are presenting. And I do also reiterate -- this is my closing comment -- the passage in the B92 report yesterday, the quote from Peter Scheider, the president from the Council of Europe that "the Tribunal should show greater understanding of the political and security risks inherent in cooperation." In other words, one shouldn't simply look at the legal position in a vacuum. One should and is entitled to, and high international officials are suggesting that this Tribunal should look at other wider factors. And in my submission, when you put those matters together, they all point to this defendant being a very good risk for this Tribunal in terms of the grant of provisional release, and I would invite you to adopt that course. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll consider these submissions and give our decision in due course. We'll sit in the next case in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
